Virtue. In philosophy, virtue is a settled excellence of character—a stable disposition to act, think, and feel in ways that are admirable and conducive to human flourishing. Aristotle defined virtue as the mean between extremes. Courage, for instance, is the mean between cowardice and recklessness. He argued that virtue is cultivated through habit and practice until the virtuous person acts rightly without deliberation. Virtue-centered ethics has experienced a renaissance in modern philosophy as an alternative to rule-based and consequence-based approaches, emphasizing that ethics is ultimately about becoming a good person, not just following rules or maximizing outcomes.

Aristotle identified two types of virtue: intellectual virtues like wisdom, understanding, and prudence, cultivated through teaching, and moral virtues like courage, temperance, justice, and generosity, cultivated through habituation and practice. The doctrine of the mean states that virtue lies between vice and excess. Courage is the mean between cowardice and rashness. Generosity is the mean between stinginess and profligacy. This applies to feelings as well as actions. Feeling anger at appropriate times, toward appropriate people, in appropriate amounts is virtue. Chronic rage or total passivity are both vicious.

For Aristotle, virtue is not innate but acquired through repeated practice. We become brave by performing brave acts, temperate by practicing self-control, just by acting justly. The virtuous person eventually performs virtuous acts effortlessly and with pleasure, not from duty or fear. Plato treated virtue as unified and intellectual. The virtuous person possesses knowledge of the Good, a transcendent form. If they truly know what is good, they will do it. Vice results from ignorance, not malice or weakness of will.

The Stoics held that virtue is the only true good and the sole path to happiness. External things like health, wealth, and reputation are preferred indifferents—nice to have but not essential to flourishing. A virtuous slave is happier than a vicious king. The Cynics embraced virtue in the form of freedom from desire. They rejected social conventions, lived ascetically, and cultivated virtue as liberation from dependence on others' approval—an extreme form of virtue as self-mastery.

Epicurus and his followers defined virtue not as asceticism but as prudent pleasure-seeking. A virtuous life involves choosing pleasures that lead to lasting satisfaction, like simple food, reliable friendships, and philosophical conversation, over fleeting indulgences that bring pain. Modern virtue ethics, through philosophers like Philippa Foot, Rosalind Hursthouse, and Alasdair MacIntyre, has revived Aristotelian ethics as a third way. Virtue ethics asks what kind of person one should be, not what rules to follow or what outcomes to maximize. It makes character central to moral philosophy and emphasizes that ethics is inseparable from the question of how to live well.
